newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - EMU may cost UK retailers 3.5 billion pounds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EMU may cost UK retailers 3.5 billion pounds.

text.p: A single European currency could cost British retailers up to 3.5 billion pounds ($5.6 billion) if Britain joins, industry body the British Retail Consortium (BRC) said on Tuesday.
Costs include staff training, re-labelling and adjusting operating and point-of-sales systems to handle the new currency, said the BRC report.

The BRC estimated an added indirect cost of 300 million pounds from changes to the pricing of products and the impact on trading patterns where shoppers would be expected to buy more before the change over and less immediately after.
But the overall costs could be cut to 1.7 billion pounds if a number of proposals were followed, said the BRC.
Twenty-five years ago, Britain's high street shops underwent a similar upheaval when decimal currency was introduced in 1971.
"BRC is recommending that the lessons learned at that time should be heeded," said Andrew Higginson, chairman of BRC's economic affairs committee.
At the time, careful preparation and the full involvement of retailers in the conversion process ensured its success and a minimum impact on inflation, he said.
The BRC suggested costs could be cut if EMU was launched in a quiet trading period, ideally February.
January 1 is one of the busiest times of the year for British retailers who offer big discounts in New Year sales.

The euro should also be introduced in a "Big Bang" and not phased in over six months. "From our point of view that would be a nightmare," said Higginson. He told a news conference retailers wanted to avoid having to work in both currencies for an extended period.
He said retailers should be given a free hand on labelling and not be forced to display prices in old currency and new euros. This alone would cost an estimated 590 million pounds.

He said draft legislation in Brussels on labelling could force retailers to display as many as eight different prices on goods. "We need a common sense approach for the way this (EMU) is introduced. We have to avoid a huge raft of legislation," Higginson said.

Retailers would need at least three years advanced notice before switching currency. Higginson said there were proposals around to introduce the euro by October 2001, giving retailers only two years to get ready which would be hard to achieve.
"We are saying we want three years," he said.

Alastair Eperon, director of the BRC, said retailers have front-line responsibility for ensuring the successful introduction of a single currency if that is the course the government decides to pursue.

"The practical implications are huge and the costs significant, but this research shows that there are easy ways in which the process of introduction can be simplified to the benefit of consumers and retailers alike."
The study showed that there are 290,000 retail outlets in Britain, handling over eight billion cash and two billion non-cash transactions a year.

Nearly two-thirds of the outlets involved would be single store businesses. The study estimates the cost to them of adopting the euro could equal 2.6 percent of last year's turnover, against 1.1 percent for large multiples with more than 100 outlets.
"BRC is not arguing for or against EMU," Higginson said. "We commissioned a study to focus on the operational practicalities." ($1=.6264 Pound)
